name: 2025 HSC Business Studies
subject: Business Studies
instructions: The full 2025 HSC Business Studies paper, run in guided mode: you get feedback after every question. Model answers and marking points are original, written to HSC standard for study use. They are not NESA's official marking guidelines.

sections.name: Section I - Multiple choice
sections.instructions: 20 marks. Attempt Questions 1 to 20. Allow about 35 minutes for this section.

questions.prompt: 1. Which performance objective is a business trying to achieve by minimising waste in production?

choices.why: Cost as an operations performance objective involves minimising the cost of inputs, transformation processes and outputs, so eliminating waste directly lowers unit cost and supports a cost leadership position.
Flexibility is the ability to adapt processes, alter the product mix or change volume in response to changing conditions, which is about adaptability rather than reducing waste.
Speed concerns the time taken between a customer request and delivery, or throughput time; faster processing may be a side benefit of less waste, but it is not the objective being pursued.
Volume is not one of the syllabus performance objectives (quality, speed, dependability, flexibility, customisation and cost), so it cannot be the objective being achieved here.

questions.prompt: 2. A dealership customises the caravans it sells by putting solar panels on the roof. Which type of market does this business operate in?

choices.why: A mass market involves selling a standardised, undifferentiated product to as many buyers as possible, which is the opposite of customising each caravan for a specific buyer group.
A niche market is a narrow, specialised segment of a larger market, and customising caravans with solar panels targets the particular needs of that smaller group of consumers.
Production is a key business function that transforms inputs into outputs, not a type of market, so it cannot describe where the dealership operates.
A resource market involves the buying and selling of factors of production such as land, labour and capital, whereas the dealership sells a finished consumer good.

questions.prompt: 3. Which of the following is an essential component of a balance sheet?

choices.why: Assets are one of the three essential components of a balance sheet, alongside liabilities and owner's equity, and represent what the business owns at a particular point in time.
Expenses are the costs incurred in earning revenue and are reported in the income statement, which covers a period of time rather than a point in time.
Sales are revenue earned over an accounting period and belong at the top of the income statement, not on the balance sheet.
Wages are an operating expense recorded in the income statement; only wages owing but unpaid would appear on a balance sheet, and then as a current liability rather than an essential component.

questions.prompt: 4. An employee is applying for maternity leave. She is told her job will not exist when she plans to return to work. What form of discrimination may have occurred?

choices.why: Age discrimination involves treating someone less favourably because they are considered too young or too old, and nothing in the scenario relates to the employee's age.
Pregnancy and maternity are not classified as a disability under anti-discrimination law, so this does not describe the ground on which the employee has been treated unfavourably.
Racial discrimination relates to race, colour, ethnicity or national origin, none of which is a factor in the removal of this employee's position.
Discrimination on the ground of sex includes pregnancy, potential pregnancy and parental leave, and removing the job of a woman taking maternity leave breaches her right to return to her position.

questions.prompt: 5. The price of a fitness watch is advertised as on special for $159. The store usually sells this watch for $159. Which area of consumer law has been broken?

choices.why: A warranty is a promise by the seller or manufacturer to repair, replace or refund a faulty product, and no claim about the performance or repair of the watch has been broken here.
Implied conditions require goods to be of acceptable quality, fit for their stated purpose and to match their description, but the issue in this case is the price claim rather than the watch itself.
Price discrimination is charging different buyers different prices for the same product in a way that lessens competition, whereas this store is charging every customer the same $159.
Labelling the usual price of $159 as a special is deceptive and misleading advertising because it leads consumers to believe a saving exists when the price has not been reduced.

questions.prompt: 6. An international clothing brand uses Japanese fashion trends and cultural preferences in its designs and advertisements for its Japanese market. Which global marketing strategy is being used?

choices.why: Customisation, also called adaptation, modifies the product and its promotion to suit the culture, tastes and preferences of a specific overseas market, exactly as the brand does for Japan.
Standardisation uses the same product, packaging and promotional message in every market to gain economies of scale, which is the opposite of tailoring designs to Japanese trends.
Global branding involves projecting one consistent brand name, image and identity worldwide, whereas here it is the designs and advertisements themselves that are being changed for the local market.

Price and quality interaction concerns how consumers judge quality from the price charged and how a business positions itself on that basis, which is a pricing decision rather than cultural adaptation.

questions.prompt: 7. Which of the following is an essential aspect of logistics?

choices.why: Reorganising plant layout is part of facilities design and layout within the transformation process, which determines the arrangement of machinery and workflow rather than the movement of goods.

choices.t: Checking the quality of all output
choices.why: Checking the quality of all output is quality control, an inspection based approach that detects defects against standards, and it sits within quality management rather than logistics.
Logistics covers the movement and storage of goods, so assessing materials handling and packaging is an essential aspect of getting inputs and finished products through the supply chain efficiently.

choices.t: Creating a budget for new machinery and equipment
choices.why: Creating a budget for new machinery is capital expenditure planning within the finance function, and although it may support operations it is not part of logistics.

questions.prompt: 8. A business, as part of its quality management strategy, demonstrates an ongoing commitment to make its operations more efficient and effective. This is an example of which of the following?

choices.why: Quality assurance involves setting up a system of processes certified against external standards such as ISO, which is about meeting agreed criteria rather than an ongoing drive for improvement.
Quality control uses inspection and checking of output against standards to identify defects, so it corrects problems after they occur rather than committing to continual refinement.
Flexibility is an operations performance objective describing the ability to adapt processes and product mix, not one of the three approaches to quality management.
Quality improvement is a continuous, ongoing commitment by all employees to make processes more efficient and effective, which matches the strategy described.

questions.prompt: 9. A business, with a 30-day credit policy, collects accounts receivables on average every 26 days. Which objective of financial management is this business aiming to achieve?

choices.why: Efficiency is the financial management objective concerned with how well a business uses its resources, and the accounts receivable turnover ratio shows debts being collected inside the 30-day credit terms.
Growth concerns increasing the size, market share or value of the business over time, which is not what the speed of debt collection measures.
Minimisation is not a financial management objective in the syllabus, which lists profitability, growth, efficiency, liquidity and solvency, so it cannot be the objective being achieved.
Solvency is the ability to meet financial commitments in the longer term, measured by gearing and the debt to equity ratio, rather than by how quickly short-term debtors pay.

questions.prompt: 10. Which of the following lists elements of the legal framework that influences human resource management?

choices.t: Code of conduct, work health and safety, awards
choices.why: Work health and safety and awards are legal elements, but a code of conduct is a voluntary, self-regulatory document created by the business itself, so this list is not entirely legal.

choices.t: Code of conduct, work health and safety, workers compensation
choices.why: Work health and safety and workers compensation are legal requirements, however the inclusion of a code of conduct again introduces a voluntary internal policy rather than a law.

choices.t: Common law, minimum employment standards, customer contact
choices.why: Common law and minimum employment standards are part of the legal framework, but customer contact is a marketing and operations concern with no place in employment law.

choices.t: Common law, minimum employment standards, workers compensation
choices.why: Common law governs the employer and employee contract and duty of care, minimum employment standards set out entitlements such as leave and hours, and workers compensation covers injured employees, so all three are elements of the legal framework influencing human resource management.

questions.prompt: 11. What is a benefit of using internal recruitment for a senior management position?

choices.t: The position will always be filled.
choices.why: Internal recruitment gives no guarantee that a suitably skilled internal candidate exists. A senior management role may remain unfilled and force the business into an external search anyway.

choices.t: It encourages staff to seek professional growth.
choices.why: Promoting from within demonstrates that career advancement is achievable, motivating staff to pursue professional development and improving morale and staff retention.

choices.t: There is a larger pool of applicants to choose from.
choices.why: This confuses internal with external recruitment. The internal pool is by definition smaller because it is restricted to current employees only.

choices.t: The business can gain perspectives from outside of the business.
choices.why: Gaining fresh ideas and outside perspectives is a benefit of external recruitment. Internal appointees bring existing organisational thinking rather than new external insight.

questions.prompt: 12. A business is introducing leading edge technology and is experiencing employee resistance. What is the most likely reason for this resistance to change?

choices.why: Staff fear deskilling, retrenchment and an inability to cope with unfamiliar systems, which is the classic employee source of resistance to change.
Redundancy payments are a financial cost borne by the business when restructuring. They are an expense of managing change, not a reason employees resist it.
Increased financial costs, such as purchase and retraining costs, explain inertia among managers and owners rather than resistance from employees.
Reorganisation of plant layout is an operations strategy that may follow new technology. It is a consequence of the change, not the underlying reason for employee resistance.

questions.prompt: 13. A marketing manager recognises that poor customer service has negatively affected sales results. In which part of the marketing process would this recognition occur?

choices.why: Identifying target markets involves segmenting consumers and selecting which groups to serve. It does not diagnose an internal weakness in service quality.
A situational analysis using SWOT and product life cycle identifies internal weaknesses such as poor customer service and links them to declining sales results.
Developing marketing strategies is the business's response to a problem, which can only occur after the analysis has identified that problem.
Establishing marketing objectives sets the goals to be achieved and follows the analysis stage. It sets targets rather than diagnosing the cause of falling sales.

questions.prompt: 14. Which of the following marketing strategies could a new gym adopt in order to attract customers and become a viable business?

choices.t: Charge a high price during the introductory stage
choices.why: Charging a high introductory price is price skimming, suited to a prestige or unique product. For an unproven new gym it deters trial and fails to build market share.

choices.t: Set an introductory price that is the same as its competitors
choices.why: Matching competitor prices gives consumers no incentive to switch to an untested business, so it does not attract the customer base a new gym needs.

choices.t: Offer a first month membership at a discount to the normal monthly fee
choices.why: A discounted first month encourages trial and builds a customer base, while the standard monthly fee that follows sustains revenue and long term viability.

choices.t: Offer a lifetime membership that is below the cost of providing the service
choices.why: Selling lifetime memberships below the cost of providing the service locks in permanent losses, so the business could attract customers yet still fail to be viable.

questions.prompt: 15. A graph of employee data is shown. What would be the most likely cause of the change in data after month 3?

choices.why: A productivity course would be expected to lift performance through improved skills, which is the opposite of the fall from 35 to 15 shown after month 3.

choices.t: Employees were given a monetary bonus.
choices.why: A monetary bonus is a financial reward that typically motivates staff, so performance would rise and absenteeism would remain low rather than quadruple.

choices.t: There was a change in senior management.
choices.why: A change in senior management introduces uncertainty, a new leadership style and possible role changes, explaining the simultaneous fall in performance and the sharp rise in both stress and absenteeism.

choices.t: Improvements in work health and safety were made.
choices.why: Improvements in work health and safety reduce hazards and workplace injury, which would lower absenteeism and stress rather than cause the sharp increases shown.

stimulus.caption: Employee data (performance, stress levels, absenteeism across months 1 to 5)

questions.prompt: 16. An extract from a business document is shown. In which month should this business have adopted cash flow management strategies?

choices.why: August is the last month with a closing balance that is not in deficit, at $0, so strategies such as distributing payments, factoring or arranging an overdraft must be implemented then to prevent the September shortfall.
September is when the $2 000 deficit actually occurs. Acting only then is reactive, because the business is already unable to meet its short term financial obligations.
November still closes at a positive $1 000, and the liquidity crisis had already occurred two months earlier, so this is far too late to be the trigger point.
December closes at $3 000, the strongest position in the projection, so there is no projected shortfall requiring cash flow strategies in that month.

stimulus.caption: Extract from a business document: cash flow, July to December

questions.prompt: 17. A chef's finger has been cut off during a workplace accident. Which of the following steps should the employer take?

choices.t: Work site is assessed for safety, then employee takes annual leave, then injury management plan is created
choices.why: Assessing the site first is correct, but directing the employee to take annual leave is wrong because a workplace injury is covered by workers compensation, not the employee's own leave entitlements.

choices.t: Injury management plan is created, then employee returns to work, then employee takes annual leave
choices.why: Creating the plan first ignores the employer's immediate WHS duty to eliminate the hazard and protect other staff, and finishing with annual leave again misuses the employee's entitlements.

choices.t: Work site is assessed for safety, then injury management plan is created, then employee is assigned suitable duties
choices.why: The employer must secure and assess the work site under WHS legislation, then create an injury management plan, then assign suitable duties as part of a structured return to work program.

choices.t: Modified work hours are organised, then injury management plan is created, then employee returns to work
choices.why: Modified hours cannot be organised before the site is made safe and before an injury management plan and medical assessment establish the worker's capacity.

stimulus.caption: Options A to D: step one, step two, step three

questions.prompt: 18. In the hope of generating long-term profit, a medical company spends $2 billion developing medicine to cure a disease. This is recorded on the company's balance sheet. Which limitation of financial reports does this demonstrate?

choices.why: Timing issues concern the period the report covers, such as selecting a favourable reporting date so the figures do not reflect typical trading performance.
Valuing assets refers to the subjective estimates used for items such as goodwill, inventory or depreciating equipment, not to how a cost is classified.
Debt repayments as a limitation refers to reports not disclosing a business's true capacity or terms for repaying its liabilities, which is not what the treatment of development costs demonstrates.
Placing research and development spending on the balance sheet capitalises an expense, inflating assets and profit and misleading users about the true financial position.

questions.prompt: 19. A retail franchise is opening a new store. Which of the following is the correct sequence for its operations process?

choices.why: Materials are a transformed input, so listing them after task design, which is part of the transformation stage, reverses the correct order of the process.
Facilities are a transforming resource input, control sits within the transformation stage, and customer service is an output, so the sequence correctly follows inputs, transformation, outputs.
Information is an input and improvement is part of transformation, but warranties are an output, so placing warranties in the middle breaks the required sequence.
Human resources and customers are both inputs, so this option never reaches the output stage and misplaces the transformation stage entirely.

questions.prompt: 20. A business calculated its gearing ratio as 75% in 2023 and 66% in 2024. Which of the following is a correct statement about the business in 2024?

choices.t: The debt to equity ratio has improved.
choices.why: Gearing is the debt to equity ratio, so a fall from 75% to 66% means less reliance on borrowed funds relative to owners' equity and a lower risk capital structure.

choices.t: There is a higher risk of business failure.
choices.why: Lower gearing reduces interest commitments and the danger of being unable to meet debt obligations, so the risk of business failure has fallen rather than increased.

choices.t: The solvency of this business has declined.
choices.why: Gearing is a measure of solvency, and a lower ratio indicates a greater ability to meet long term financial commitments, so solvency has improved, not declined.

choices.t: The owner will have a higher return-on-equity.
choices.why: Return on equity rises from greater leverage or improved profitability. Reducing gearing removes leverage, and the gearing ratio alone reveals nothing about the level of profit earned.

sections.name: Section II - Short answer
sections.instructions: 40 marks. Attempt Questions 21 to 24. Allow about 1 hour and 15 minutes for this section.

questions.prompt: Question 21 (a) Outline the corporate social responsibility demonstrated by this business.
questions.model: Corporate social responsibility means this cafe goes beyond its legal compliance obligations to consider the interests of its stakeholders and the wider community. The cafe demonstrates this by donating its left-over food to a local charity at the end of each day, which supports disadvantaged people in the community instead of sending edible food to landfill. This practice also reduces food waste, improving the cafe's environmental performance under a triple bottom line approach and building its reputation as an ethical local business.

points.text: Shows understanding of CSR as acting beyond legal compliance in the interests of stakeholders and the community
points.hint: State clearly that CSR means acting beyond what the law requires, in the interests of stakeholders and the community.

points.text: Links the cafe's specific action (donating left-over food) to a social or environmental benefit
points.hint: Name the actual practice in the stimulus, the daily food donation to charity, and say what social or environmental good it does.

stimulus.caption: Question 21 stimulus
stimulus.text: A cafe produces quality food and friendly, personalised service. It donates its left-over food to a local charity at the end of each day.

questions.prompt: Question 21 (b) Outline the difference between goods and services in this business.
questions.model: In this cafe, goods are the tangible physical outputs that a customer can see, touch and consume, such as the quality meals, cakes and coffee produced in the kitchen. Services are the intangible actions performed for the customer, such as the friendly, personalised table service the cafe is known for. Because services are intangible they are produced and consumed at the same time and cannot be stored as inventory, whereas goods can be prepared in advance and held until they are sold.

points.text: Identifies goods as tangible physical output, using a cafe example such as meals or coffee
points.hint: Say goods are tangible and give a cafe example such as the meals, cakes or coffee.

points.text: Identifies services as intangible actions, using the cafe's personalised service, and notes a key difference such as being produced and consumed simultaneously or not able to be stored
points.hint: Say services are intangible, name the cafe's friendly personalised service, and add that services cannot be stored because they are consumed as they are produced.

stimulus.caption: Question 21 stimulus
stimulus.text: A cafe produces quality food and friendly, personalised service. It donates its left-over food to a local charity at the end of each day.

questions.prompt: Question 21 (c) Explain the influence of ONE legal regulation on the operations management of this business.
questions.model: One legal regulation influencing this cafe is food safety legislation, including the Food Act 2003 (NSW) and the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code, which sets rules for how food is stored, prepared, handled and labelled. This regulation directly shapes the transformation process, because the cafe must monitor refrigeration temperatures, train all staff in safe food handling, appoint a food safety supervisor and keep cleaning and temperature records. As a result, the business faces higher compliance costs for commercial refrigeration, staff training and council inspections, and some processes take longer, which can reduce speed as a performance objective. However, complying also strengthens quality management, since consistently safe food protects customers from illness, supports the cafe's reputation for quality food and avoids fines or forced closure.

points.text: Names a specific legal regulation that applies to a cafe, such as food safety legislation, work health and safety law, environmental protection law, consumer law or council licensing
points.hint: Name an actual regulation, for example food safety legislation, the Food Act 2003 (NSW), work health and safety law or a council food licence, rather than just saying the law.

points.text: Explains the cause and effect on a specific operations process (inputs, transformation, storage, handling or staff training)
points.hint: Show cause and effect by explaining exactly what the cafe must change in its operations process, such as storage temperatures or staff training.

points.text: Explains a resulting consequence for the business, such as compliance costs, reduced speed, improved quality or avoided penalties
points.hint: Finish the chain of cause and effect with a consequence, such as higher compliance costs, better quality management or the risk of fines and closure.

stimulus.caption: Question 21 stimulus
stimulus.text: A cafe produces quality food and friendly, personalised service. It donates its left-over food to a local charity at the end of each day.

questions.prompt: Question 21 (d) The owners of the cafe would like to expand their dessert range. They plan to outsource cakes from the local bakery to sell at their cafe. Discuss the implications of outsourcing the new desserts for the operation of this business.
questions.model:
Outsourcing involves the cafe contracting an external supplier, the local bakery, to produce its desserts instead of making them in-house. One implication for operations is access to the bakery's specialist skills, commercial equipment and economies of scale, which should deliver consistently high quality cakes that match the cafe's existing reputation for quality food. The cafe also avoids the capital cost of ovens, extra kitchen space and a qualified pastry chef, and can expand its dessert range quickly, improving flexibility while staff stay focused on core food production and personalised service.

However, outsourcing reduces the cafe's control over quality and supply. If the bakery delivers late, changes its recipes or lowers its standards, the cafe cannot meet customer demand and its reputation suffers, so it must manage the supplier relationship through clear contracts, agreed quality standards and regular checks. The bakery also adds its own profit margin to the price, so the cafe earns less on each dessert than if it produced them itself, and it has limited ability to customise cakes for individual customer requests.

On balance, outsourcing to a trusted local bakery suits this cafe because the quality and cost savings outweigh the risks, provided supply reliability and quality are closely monitored.

points.text: Shows understanding of outsourcing as contracting an external supplier (the local bakery) to perform part of the operations function
points.hint: Open by making clear that outsourcing means the cafe pays an external supplier, the local bakery, to do work it would otherwise do in-house.

points.text: Discusses at least one positive implication for operations, such as specialist expertise, avoided capital costs, faster expansion of the product range or improved flexibility
points.hint: Add a clear argument for outsourcing, such as gaining the bakery's expertise and equipment without buying ovens or hiring a pastry chef.

points.text: Discusses at least one negative implication, such as loss of control over quality or supply, dependence on the supplier, or a reduced profit margin
points.hint: Add a clear argument against outsourcing, such as losing control over quality and supply, late deliveries, or losing profit margin to the bakery.

points.text: Sustains the argument by linking implications to this cafe's quality food and personalised service, and reaches a weighed conclusion
points.hint: Tie the discussion back to this cafe's reputation and personalised service, and close with a short weighed judgement that says which side outweighs the other.

stimulus.caption: Question 21 stimulus
stimulus.text: A cafe produces quality food and friendly, personalised service. It donates its left-over food to a local charity at the end of each day.

questions.prompt: Question 22 (a) Identify ONE weakness and ONE potential threat for this business.
questions.model: One weakness is the poor quality of the product, because the stainless steel bottles leak, which is an internal factor. One potential threat is competitors selling leak-proof bottles in biodegradable packaging, which is an external factor.

points.text: Identifies a valid internal weakness, such as the leaking bottles, poor product quality or non-biodegradable packaging
points.hint: Name one internal weakness, for example that the bottles leak, and make clear it is a factor inside the business.

points.text: Identifies a valid external threat, such as competitors, changing consumer preferences for sustainability, negative reviews or government regulation
points.hint: Name one external threat, such as competitors offering leak-proof bottles in biodegradable packaging, or changing consumer preferences.

stimulus.caption: Question 22 stimulus
stimulus.text: A business sells stainless steel water bottles. However, customers have complained that the bottles leak, and that they do not come in biodegradable packaging.

questions.prompt: Question 22 (b) Justify TWO product strategies that could be implemented by this business to gain a competitive advantage.
questions.model:
The first product strategy is product differentiation through redesign and value adding: the business should re-engineer the lid with a silicone seal and screw thread so the bottle is genuinely leak-proof, and back it with a lifetime warranty. This is justified because the leaking is the direct cause of customer complaints, so fixing it removes the main reason customers switch to rivals. A guaranteed leak-proof bottle becomes a clear point of difference that lets the business charge a premium price, cut costly returns and build repeat purchase and brand loyalty, which is a sustainable competitive advantage.

The second product strategy is changing the packaging to biodegradable, plastic free materials carrying a recognised environmental certification. This is justified because it responds directly to the second complaint and to growing socio-cultural demand for sustainable products, positioning the brand as the environmentally responsible choice in the reusable bottle market. Green packaging strengthens brand image, attracts environmentally conscious consumers away from competitors and increases market share, while also protecting the business from future government regulation on single use plastics, so the gain in reputation clearly outweighs the higher packaging cost.

points.text: Names and describes a first product strategy, such as product differentiation or value adding through redesigning the leaking bottle
points.hint: Name a recognised product strategy, such as product differentiation or value adding, and describe the actual change to the bottle.

points.text: Justifies the first strategy with reasons linked to competitive advantage, such as removing complaints, creating a point of difference, premium pricing or repeat purchase
points.hint: Give reasons why this strategy works, linking it to the customer complaints, a point of difference, premium pricing and repeat purchase.

points.text: Names and describes a second product strategy, such as biodegradable or recyclable packaging and environmentally friendly branding
points.hint: Add a second, different product strategy, for example changing to biodegradable, recyclable or plastic free packaging.

points.text: Justifies the second strategy with reasons linked to competitive advantage, such as meeting consumer demand for sustainability, improved brand image or increased market share
points.hint: Explain why the second strategy pays off, linking sustainability demand to brand image and market share.

stimulus.caption: Question 22 stimulus
stimulus.text: A business sells stainless steel water bottles. However, customers have complained that the bottles leak, and that they do not come in biodegradable packaging.

questions.prompt: Question 22 (c) Why is it important for this business to monitor and control its marketing strategies?
questions.model:
Monitoring means checking and recording the actual performance of the marketing plan against its objectives, using data such as sales figures, market share, product returns and customer complaints. This is important because it allows the business to detect problems early, and the complaints about leaking bottles and non-biodegradable packaging are evidence that the current product is not satisfying the target market.

Controlling means comparing that actual performance with planned performance and then taking corrective action. This matters because once the business sees that sales have fallen short of the forecast, it can revise the marketing mix, for example by redesigning the lid or switching to biodegradable packaging, before the problem grows.

This process is important because it stops the business wasting marketing expenditure on strategies that are not working, protects its brand reputation and market share against competitors, and keeps the business responsive to changing customer needs, improving long term profitability.

points.text: Explains monitoring as checking actual performance against the marketing objectives using data such as sales, market share or customer complaints, AND gives the reason this matters, for example detecting the leaking bottle complaints early
points.hint: Do not stop at the definition. Say that actual performance is tracked against the objectives using data such as sales figures or complaints, then give the reason: problems are picked up before they grow.

points.text: Explains controlling as comparing actual with planned performance and taking corrective action, AND gives the benefit, for example revising the marketing mix before sales fall further
points.hint: Again pair the definition with a reason: comparing actual with planned results lets the business take corrective action, such as redesigning the lid or changing the packaging, before more sales are lost.

points.text: Explains why this matters for the business, for example avoiding wasted marketing expenditure, protecting brand reputation and market share, or staying responsive to customer needs
points.hint: Finish by saying what the business gains, such as avoiding wasted marketing spend and protecting its reputation and market share.

stimulus.caption: Question 22 stimulus
stimulus.text: A business sells stainless steel water bottles. However, customers have complained that the bottles leak, and that they do not come in biodegradable packaging.

questions.prompt: Question 23 (a) What does the expense ratio for 2024 indicate for this business?
questions.model: The expense ratio for 2024 is 30%, calculated as 210 000 ÷ 700 000 × 100. This indicates that 30 cents in every sales dollar is now absorbed by expenses. The ratio has risen sharply from 23.3% in 2023 and sits well above the 2024 industry average of 20%, showing that total expenses have grown faster than sales as the business expanded into several countries. Therefore the ratio indicates weakening expense control and reduced cost efficiency, which explains why net profit rose only slightly despite a $100 000 increase in sales, and signals a threat to future profitability if costs are not minimised.

points.text: States the 2024 expense ratio as 30% (210 000 divided by 700 000 times 100)
points.hint: Show the figure and the working: 210 000 ÷ 700 000 × 100 = 30%.

points.text: Indicates what the figure means, comparing it with the 2023 ratio of 23.3% or the 2024 industry average of 20% and linking the rise to weaker expense control, cost efficiency and profitability
points.hint: A ratio means little on its own, so compare it with 2023 (23.3%) and the industry average (20%), then say what the rise means for expense control and profitability.

stimulus.caption: Question 23 stimulus: a travel agency focused on expanding its sales in several countries

questions.prompt: Question 23 (b) How can undertaking a comparative ratio analysis improve this business's financial outcome?
questions.model:
Comparative ratio analysis involves comparing a business's ratios over different time periods, against budgeted standards, against similar businesses and against industry averages, so that raw figures become useful information for decision making.

Comparing 2023 with 2024 shows the expense ratio climbing from 23.3% to 30% while the industry average fell to 20%. Identifying this gap allows management to investigate the cause, such as the cost of expanding sales into several countries, and to apply expense minimisation strategies like renegotiating supplier contracts and reducing discretionary marketing, which improves net profit.

Comparison over time also shows the debt to equity ratio rising from 0.6:1 to 1:1 while the industry has remained at 0.6:1. Recognising that the agency is now more highly geared than its competitors allows it to reduce reliance on borrowed funds by using retained profits or equity finance, lowering interest expense and improving solvency and long term stability.

Finally, a return on equity of 8.5% against an industry average of 12% signals that owners' funds are underperforming. Because comparative analysis benchmarks performance against realistic standards, it allows the business to set achievable financial objectives, monitor them and take corrective action, thereby improving financial outcomes such as profitability, efficiency and growth.

points.text: Explains what comparative ratio analysis is: comparing over time, against standards, similar businesses and industry averages
points.hint: Define comparative ratio analysis first: comparison over different time periods, against budgeted standards, similar businesses and industry averages.

points.text: Uses the expense ratio comparison (23.3% to 30% against 20%) to show how cost control improves profitability
points.hint: Use the stimulus data: link the rising expense ratio to expense minimisation strategies and improved net profit.

points.text: Uses the debt to equity comparison (rising from 0.6:1 to 1:1 against an industry average of 0.6:1) to show that identifying higher gearing lets the business reduce reliance on debt and improve solvency
points.hint: The gearing has worsened, so explain how spotting that lets the business restructure its finance and improve solvency.

points.text: Links benchmarking (return on equity 8.5% against 12%) to informed decision making, realistic financial objectives and corrective action
points.hint: Finish by explaining how benchmarking informs decision making, goal setting and corrective action to improve financial outcomes.

stimulus.caption: Question 23 stimulus: a travel agency focused on expanding its sales in several countries

questions.prompt: Question 23 (c) Explain how TWO global market influences could affect the solvency of this business.
questions.model:
Global market influences are external factors that shape a business's access to finance and its cost, and solvency is the ability to meet long term financial commitments, measured by the debt to equity ratio.

Firstly, interest rates are the cost of borrowing funds. This travel agency has increased its debt to equity ratio from 0.6:1 to 1:1, which is above the industry average of 0.6:1, so it is heavily reliant on borrowed funds. If global interest rates rise, its interest repayments increase, absorbing a greater share of net profit and leaving less retained profit available to repay principal. Its ability to meet long term commitments therefore falls, so solvency declines and the risk of default increases.

Secondly, the availability of funds refers to the ease with which the business can access finance on international financial markets. When global credit tightens, lenders apply stricter lending criteria and demand higher risk premiums. Because the agency is already highly geared and its expense ratio has risen to 30%, lenders may classify it as high risk and restrict further funding. The business could then be forced into expensive short term finance to continue its overseas expansion, which worsens its gearing and further reduces long term solvency.

points.text: Identifies TWO global market influences using syllabus language, such as interest rates, availability of funds or the economic outlook
points.hint: Name two influences in syllabus terms: interest rates, availability of funds or economic outlook.

points.text: Explains a clear cause and effect chain for the first influence (higher rates, higher repayments, less retained profit)
points.hint: Explain means show cause and effect, so trace the chain from the influence through to the business's finances.

points.text: Links the explanation directly to the debt to equity data (0.6:1 rising to 1:1) and the ability to meet long term commitments
points.hint: Keep returning to the ability to meet long term commitments: use the debt to equity movement from 0.6:1 to 1:1 as evidence.

points.text: Explains a second, distinct influence with its own effect on the business's ability to meet long term commitments
points.hint: Develop your second influence just as fully as the first rather than only naming it.

stimulus.caption: Question 23 stimulus: a travel agency focused on expanding its sales in several countries

questions.prompt: Question 24 (a) Describe the influence technology has on the human resources function.
questions.model:
Technology is a major influence on human resources because it changes both the nature of work and the way human resource processes are carried out.

Automation and computerisation replace routine manual tasks, so a business needs fewer employees with lower level skills and more employees with technical skills. This creates a need for retraining and upskilling, and can also lead to deskilling, redundancies and the restructuring of job roles.

Technology also changes work arrangements. Laptops, video conferencing and cloud based systems support telecommuting and flexible hours, which improves work life balance and widens the labour market beyond one location, although it can blur the boundary between work and home and weaken team cohesion.

Human resource processes themselves become faster and more efficient. E-recruitment, online applications and testing, human resource information systems, e-learning and electronic performance monitoring reduce administration costs and improve record keeping, although electronic surveillance raises employee privacy concerns that managers must handle carefully to maintain a positive workplace culture.

points.text: Describes how technology changes the nature of work and skill requirements (automation, upskilling, retraining, redundancy)
points.hint: Describe the change to the work itself: automation removes routine tasks and creates a need for retraining or redundancies.

points.text: Describes changed work arrangements such as telecommuting, flexible hours and work life balance
points.hint: Add a feature about work arrangements, for example telecommuting and flexible hours.

points.text: Describes technology in human resource processes (e-recruitment, HRIS, e-learning, electronic monitoring) and a resulting effect
points.hint: Include features of the HR processes themselves, such as e-recruitment, HRIS or electronic performance monitoring, and their effect.

questions.prompt: Question 24 (b) Employees at a factory have been discouraged by their employers from joining a union. Explain TWO possible reasons for this.
questions.model:
One reason is to keep labour costs down and retain managerial control over wages and conditions. Unions bargain collectively on behalf of their members and typically press for higher wages, improved conditions and stricter application of awards. If the workforce remains non-unionised, the employer can negotiate directly with individual employees or through its own enterprise agreement, so wage outcomes stay closer to minimum standards, labour costs remain lower and profitability is protected.

A second reason is to reduce the risk of industrial action and disputes. Unions can organise strikes, work bans, picketing and stop work meetings, which halt production at the factory, delay orders, damage the business's reputation and increase costs. Without union involvement, management can also introduce changes such as new technology or altered shift patterns with less collective resistance, so the factory remains flexible and productive.

Although these reasons benefit the employer, pressuring employees not to join a union may amount to adverse action or coercion under the general protections provisions of the Fair Work Act 2009, which protect freedom of association.

points.text: Explains a first reason based on labour costs and managerial control over bargaining
points.hint: One clear reason is cost: unions bargain collectively for higher wages, so a non-unionised workforce keeps labour costs lower.

points.text: Explains a second reason based on avoiding industrial action, disputes and disruption to production
points.hint: Add a second distinct reason, such as avoiding strikes, work bans and disruption to production.

points.text: Shows cause and effect by linking each reason to a business consequence such as lower costs, fewer disruptions or greater flexibility to introduce change
points.hint: Explain means show the link, so state the consequence for the business, not just the reason.

questions.prompt: Question 24 (c) A business pays migrant workers less, and bullies staff members. Explain how this business is engaging in illegal practices.
questions.model:
Paying migrant workers less than other employees for the same work is both underpayment and unlawful discrimination. Every employee is entitled to the national minimum wage and to the pay rates and entitlements set out in the relevant modern award and the National Employment Standards under the Fair Work Act 2009. Paying below these rates because of a worker's race or national origin also breaches anti-discrimination legislation such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 and the NSW Anti-Discrimination Act 1977, which require equal employment opportunity for all staff. The Fair Work Ombudsman can therefore investigate, order back payment of wages and impose significant penalties, and the business risks reputational damage that harms recruitment and sales.

Bullying staff members breaches work health and safety legislation, because the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) imposes a duty of care on the employer to provide a workplace that is safe and without risks to health, including psychological health. Repeated unreasonable behaviour that creates a risk to health is workplace bullying, and affected employees may apply to the Fair Work Commission for a stop bullying order. The employer may also be held vicariously liable for the conduct of its managers. Consequently the business could face prosecution by SafeWork NSW, workers compensation claims for psychological injury, higher premiums and high staff turnover.

points.text: Explains that underpayment breaches minimum employment standards, the modern award or the Fair Work Act
points.hint: Name the legal source of the breach: the national minimum wage, the modern award and the National Employment Standards.

points.text: Identifies discrimination against migrant workers as a breach of anti-discrimination and equal employment opportunity law, naming legislation
points.hint: Paying migrant workers less on the basis of race is discrimination, so name anti-discrimination legislation and EEO.

points.text: Explains that bullying breaches the employer's work health and safety duty of care, including psychological health
points.hint: Link bullying to the WHS duty of care to provide a safe workplace, including psychological safety.

points.text: Explains the consequences and enforcement, such as Fair Work Ombudsman action, penalties, back pay, workers compensation or reputational damage
points.hint: Finish each breach with its consequence: investigation, penalties, back pay, compensation claims or reputational damage.

sections.name: Section III - Business report
sections.instructions: 20 marks. Attempt Question 25. Allow about 35 minutes. Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate knowledge and understanding relevant to the question; apply the hypothetical business situation; communicate using relevant business terminology and concepts; present a sustained, logical and cohesive response in the form of a business report.

questions.prompt:
Question 25. You have been hired as a consultant by the owner to write a business report. In your report:
• outline ONE relevant human resource management process that the business could use
• describe the purpose of the above chart and any issues found in the chart
• recommend appropriate global factors the business can use to achieve cost leadership.
questions.model:
A Band 6 response is presented as a genuine business report: a title, a short introduction naming the consultant role and the purpose, headed sections that mirror the three bullets, and a brief conclusion, with the three sections at roughly a third of the report each.

The first section outlines ONE human resource management process. Acquisition is the most logical choice, because the business must analyse the staffing needs of the overseas plant, carry out job analysis and job design, then recruit internally or externally and select employees using interviews, testing and reference checks. Separation is an equally valid choice, because closing the Australian factory means both voluntary and involuntary separation, so the section would outline redundancy entitlements, notice periods and consultation with affected employees. Whichever process is chosen, it is outlined in general terms and then tied back to the relocation.

The second section describes the Gantt chart as a scheduling tool that sequences activities across a time line, shows the duration of each task and where tasks overlap, and lets management coordinate resources and monitor progress against the deadline. It then exposes the four strongest faults. The Build new factory bar spans only December, an unrealistic duration for constructing an overseas manufacturing facility, so the schedule underestimates lead time and the 2026 deadline cannot be met. Manufacturing begins in November, a full month before construction even starts, and the December manufacturing bar overlaps the build rather than following it. The Australian factory closes in October while the new plant is not ready until December, creating a production gap that risks lost sales and lost customers. Staffing needs are determined from January to March, after production was scheduled to begin, so the new plant would have no workforce.

The final section recommends global factors and gives reasons in favour of each, tied to a stated reason for relocating. Global sourcing from the new Asian suppliers is recommended because it lowers input costs and shortens lead times, which directly answers the high cost of Australian production. Economies of scale from one larger overseas plant are recommended because fixed costs are spread over greater output, so unit cost falls and price can be reduced without cutting the margin. Scanning and learning is recommended because benchmarking against global best practice transfers proven methods into the business, correcting the poor product quality that is driving customers away. Research and development is recommended because redesigning both the product and the production process cuts waste and rework, lowering unit cost while positioning the business to supply the potential Asian growth market. Each recommendation therefore supports cost leadership with a stated reason, as the directive requires.
scaffold: Set the report format up before writing a sentence: a title such as Relocation Report for XYZ Equipment Pty Ltd, a two sentence introduction stating your role as consultant and the purpose of the report, three headings taken straight from the three bullets, then a short conclusion.

Choose ONE human resource process and outline it in general terms, linked to the relocation: acquisition (analysing staffing needs, job analysis and job design, recruitment and selection of overseas staff) or separation (voluntary and involuntary separation, including redundancy entitlements, notice and consultation for the Australian employees when the factory closes).

Describe the purpose of the chart before criticising it: a Gantt chart schedules and sequences activities across a time line, shows the duration of each task and where tasks overlap, and lets management coordinate resources and monitor progress against the deadline.

Read the chart month by month and name the month and the consequence every time. Lead with the strongest fault, which is duration: the Build new factory bar spans only December, an unrealistic duration for constructing an overseas manufacturing facility, so the schedule underestimates lead time and the 2026 deadline cannot be met. Then add that manufacturing begins in November, a full month before construction even starts, and the December manufacturing bar overlaps the build rather than following it; that the Australian factory closes in October while the new plant is not ready until December, leaving a production gap; and that staffing needs are settled from January to March, after production was scheduled to begin. If you have room, add that the warehouse is leased in February after the goods are made and the business name is registered in March rather than first.

Recommend global factors for cost leadership and give a reason in favour of each, tying it to one of the stated reasons for relocating: global sourcing from the new Asian suppliers lowers input costs and shortens lead times, answering the high cost of Australian production; economies of scale from one larger overseas plant spread fixed costs over greater output, so unit cost falls; scanning and learning benchmarks the operation against global best practice and transfers proven methods, correcting the poor product quality; and research and development redesigns the product and the process to cut waste and rework while positioning the business for the potential Asian growth market. State the reason every time, because Recommend means provide reasons in favour.

Finish with a short conclusion restating the priority order of tasks and the 2026 deadline, and check that business terminology appears in every section. Aim for roughly 900 to 1200 words in full report format, split about evenly across the three headed sections, since each bullet carries equal weight in the marking criteria.

stimulus.caption: Relocation plan for XYZ Equipment Pty Ltd 2025-2026
stimulus.text: XYZ Equipment Pty Ltd is an Australian business which manufactures equipment for Australian schools. The business would like to relocate and manufacture overseas by the beginning of 2026 for the following reasons: labour and production costs in Australia are too high; product is of poor quality; Australia has strict environmental laws; there is a potential growth market in Asia.

sections.name: Section IV - Extended response
sections.instructions: 20 marks. Attempt EITHER Question 26 OR Question 27. Allow about 35 minutes. Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate knowledge and understanding relevant to the question; apply relevant business case study/studies and contemporary business issues; communicate using relevant business terminology and concepts; present a sustained, logical and cohesive response.

questions.prompt: Explain how target markets affect e-marketing, people, processes and physical evidence.
questions.model: A Band 6 response sustains one argument: the characteristics of the chosen target market drive every marketing strategy decision, so it explains cause and effect rather than listing strategies. It defines target market and the segmentation used to identify it, demographic, geographic, psychographic and behavioural, and distinguishes a mass market approach from a niche market approach. It also makes clear that people, processes and physical evidence extend the marketing mix, while e-marketing is a separate marketing strategy in its own right rather than part of that mix. Each of the four required elements is then related back to the market. E-marketing: the market's age, income and online behaviour determine whether the business uses social media, an app, personalised email, data mining or influencer content, and where it advertises. People: a premium market requires highly trained, product knowledgeable staff, while a mass market prioritises speed and consistency, which reshapes recruitment, training and service standards. Processes: booking systems, self service technology, order tracking and delivery speed are designed around what the target market values. Physical evidence: store layout, ambience, packaging, uniforms and website design supply the tangible cues that match market expectations and reinforce positioning. Judgement is not required, but at least one real business case study is integrated throughout, alongside contemporary issues such as data privacy, artificial intelligence chatbots and the growth of e-commerce.
scaffold: Write a thesis you can return to in every paragraph: the target market a business identifies determines the design of its e-marketing, people, processes and physical evidence, because each element exists to meet that market's expectations.
Open by defining target market and outlining how it is identified through market segmentation (demographic, geographic, psychographic, behavioural) and through a mass market or niche market approach.

Choose one or two real businesses as case study evidence, picking a business whose target market you can state precisely, goods or services, since physical evidence and processes apply to retailers and manufacturers as well. Write down their exact target market before you start, so every example stays consistent.

Give a developed paragraph to each of the four elements in turn. In each paragraph name the market characteristic first, then the strategy it causes, then the effect on the business, since the verb Explain demands the relationship be made clear.
Weave contemporary business issues through the paragraphs: e-commerce growth, data collection and privacy, artificial intelligence chatbots, personalisation and social media influencers.
Conclude by restating the causal relationship rather than summarising. Aim for roughly 900 to 1200 words across five or six paragraphs.
questions.label: Question 26

questions.prompt: Explain how financial strategies can achieve liquidity and profitability objectives.
questions.model: A Band 6 response explains cause and effect: each financial strategy is linked to a specific objective and to the ratio that measures it, and liquidity and profitability receive roughly equal weight. Liquidity is defined as the ability to meet short term financial commitments and is measured by the current ratio. The response explains cash flow management, including distribution of payments, discounts for early payment and factoring, and working capital management, including control of current assets (cash, receivables, inventories), control of current liabilities (payables, loans, overdrafts), leasing and sale and lease back, showing for each whether it improves the timing and availability of cash or genuinely changes the current ratio by altering current assets or current liabilities. Profitability is defined as maximising return relative to sales and to owners' equity, measured by the gross profit ratio, net profit ratio and return on equity. The response explains cost controls, including fixed and variable costs, cost centres and expense minimisation, and revenue controls, including pricing policy, sales mix and sales objectives. It also recognises tension between the objectives, since leasing improves liquidity but adds an ongoing expense that lowers profit. Real case study evidence and contemporary influences such as interest rates and hedging are integrated throughout.
scaffold: Define both objectives in the introduction and name their measures: liquidity as the ability to pay short term debts, measured by the current ratio; profitability as maximising return, measured by the gross profit ratio, net profit ratio and return on equity.
Plan a balanced structure, roughly half the response on strategies that achieve liquidity and half on strategies that achieve profitability, because the question requires both.

For liquidity, explain cash flow management (distribution of payments, discounts for early payment, factoring) and working capital management (control of current assets and current liabilities, leasing, sale and lease back), stating for each whether it improves the timing of cash inflows and outflows (distribution of payments, discounts for early payment, factoring) or actually shifts the current ratio by changing current assets or current liabilities (sale and lease back converting a non-current asset to cash, leasing avoiding a large cash outlay, reducing overdrafts and payables). Remember that control of current assets means holding optimal, not maximum, levels of cash, receivables and inventories, because excess inventory ties up working capital.

For profitability, explain cost controls (fixed and variable costs, cost centres, expense minimisation) and revenue controls (marketing objectives, sales objectives, sales mix, pricing policy), stating for each how it moves the expense ratio, net profit ratio or return on equity.

Attach a real business case study example to each strategy and bring in contemporary influences such as interest rates, exchange rate movements and hedging, since global financial management affects both objectives.
Devote a paragraph to the trade off between the two objectives, then conclude on how the strategies work together. Aim for roughly 900 to 1200 words.
